python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='engine/api.py'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('''@app.get("/api/ride/pois")''',
'''@app.post("/api/ride/discover")
def ride_discover(body: dict):
    """Plan a loop that goes to a road this rider has never ridden.

    The fog map's whole point is to end in a ride. Same cost function, same
    escape-the-city behaviour, one forced stop: the road they picked.
    """
    rider = (body.get("rider") or "A").upper()
    p = get_profile(rider)
    minutes = float(body.get("minutes") or p.get("typical_ride_min") or 150)
    target = body.get("target")
    if not target or len(target) != 2:
        raise HTTPException(400, "target must be [lat, lon]")
    origin_ll = body.get("origin") or [p["home"]["lat"], p["home"]["lon"]]
    if not (_in_bbox(origin_ll) and _in_bbox(target)):
        raise HTTPException(400, "origin or target is outside the cached road tiles")

    g = get_road_graph()
    cg = get_cell_graph()
    cost = _croads.RoadCost(
        g, _cells.Cost(cg, _cells.Rider(cg, ridden=p.get("ridden_squares"),
                                        lean_p95=p.get("lean_ceiling") or 35.0)),
        escape=bool(body.get("escape", True)))
    origin = g.nearest_node(*origin_ll)
    stop_node = g.nearest_node(*target)
    if origin is None or stop_node is None:
        raise HTTPException(400, "could not snap to a road")

    stop = {"name": body.get("name") or "your new road", "kind": "unridden",
            "node": stop_node, "lat": target[0], "lon": target[1],
            "weight": 1.0}
    got = _scenic._ride(g, cost, get_scenic_index(), origin, [stop],
                        float(body.get("alpha", 3.0)), minutes * 60.0, 1)
    if not got or not got["routes"]:
        raise HTTPException(
            404, "That road will not fit inside this much time. Try longer.")

    r = got["routes"][0]
    r["label"] = stop["name"]
    return {
        "rider": rider, "minutes": minutes, "kind": "discover",
        "origin": list(g.node_pos(origin)),
        "lean_ceiling": p.get("lean_ceiling"),
        "excluded_segments": sum(1 for seg in g.segments if cost.excluded(seg)),
        "total_segments": len(g.segments),
        "routes": [{k: r[k] for k in
                    ("label", "coords", "kpis", "roads", "stops", "legs",
                     "visited", "value_thirds", "urban_share")}],
    }


@app.get("/api/ride/pois")''')
open(p,'w').write(s)
PYEOF

def _ride(g, cost, index, origin, ordered, alpha, budget, max_stops,
          rider_id="A", profile_ratings=None):
    """Walk the chain: one goal-directed leg per stop, then home.

    Roads already used are charged four times over on later legs -- BMW's own
    `alreadyUsedRoads` -- so the way back is not a rerun of the way out.
    """
    if not ordered:
        return None
    segs: list[int] = []
    used: set[int] = set()
    retraced: set[int] = set()
    node = origin
    legs = []
    for s in ordered:
        part = _leg(g, cost, node, s["node"], alpha, used)
        if not part:
            return None
        retraced |= set(part) & used
        segs += part
        used |= set(part)
        legs.append({"to": s["name"], "kind": s["kind"],
                     "km": round(sum(float(g.by_id[x]["length_m"])
                                     for x in part) / 1000, 1)})
        node = s["node"]

    home = _leg(g, cost, node, origin, alpha, used)
    if not home:
        return None
    retraced |= set(home) & used
    segs += home
    legs.append({"to": "home", "kind": "return",
                 "km": round(sum(float(g.by_id[x]["length_m"])
                                 for x in home) / 1000, 1)})

content.text:
Done and pushed (`7188352`, on top of PR #12's branch). Reload **http://127.0.0.1:8001/ride**.

## The bug

Planning a ride while the fog was up left the map in **both states at once**. `#mapStage.globe-ready.route-active #globe` outranks my `.fog-active` rule on CSS specificity, so the globe came back over a map still covered in fog lines.

Fog and route are two *views* of the same map, not layers of one. They're now mutually exclusive: turning fog on clears the route, and planning a ride leaves the fog view. Verified in the browser — fog up, picked Monday's window, planned, and it dropped cleanly to a 49.2 km route.

## Green and red

**Green means ridden, full stop** — not "ridden and scenic". A road you've been down is yours whether or not it scored well, and shading it by quality would answer a different question than the one the fog map asks.

**Red means good and unridden.** Scored with the same function the router uses, so what glows red is exactly what the planner would send you down if you asked. The cutoff is the 80th percentile of *that rider's own* unridden set rather than a fixed score, so it stays a shortlist whether someone has ridden 10% of the region or 90%. Rider A has **142 km** of it.

## The prompt

*"Fancy somewhere new today?"* with the unridden-kilometre count and a button that lights the fog and takes you to the best of them.

## One thing I could not make work, and did not fake

I built `/api/ride/discover` to plan a loop **through** a chosen unridden road, by pinning it as the anchor of a normal scenic chain. The pinning works — it's tried first. But PR #10's chain builder rejects any loop retracing more than 10% of itself, and **no loop through a single specified road fits**, for either rider, at any budget up to five hours. I raised the limit to 22% for this case specifically; still nothing.

That guard is correct for a ride the planner invented, and it's arguably too strict for a road the rider named — but changing it further is a call on *your* quality bar, not mine, so I stopped.

What I did fix is worse than the limitation: before I added a check, discover **silently returned a different destination**. Ask for Dorfstraße, get Bismarckturm Assenhausen, no mention. It now returns *"No loop through X fits in N minutes"* instead. The prompt therefore takes you to the road on the map rather than routing you down it.

If you want it to actually route there, the options are to relax `MAX_RETRACE_SHARE` further for rider-chosen destinations, or to allow the discover loop more stops so it has room to come home a different way. Say which and I'll do it.

class ScenicIndex:
    """POIs snapped onto the road graph, once."""

    def __init__(self, graph: RoadGraph, pois: list[dict]):
        self.g = graph
        self.pois = []
        viewpoints = [p for p in pois if p.get("kind") == "viewpoint"]
        for p in pois:
            target = p
            target_source = "lake road access" if p.get("kind") == "lake" else "poi"
            if p.get("kind") == "lake" and viewpoints:
                nearby = sorted(
                    viewpoints,
                    key=lambda v: haversine_m((p["lat"], p["lon"]),
                                              (v["lat"], v["lon"])),
                )
                for candidate in nearby:
                    if haversine_m((p["lat"], p["lon"]),
                                   (candidate["lat"], candidate["lon"])) > LAKE_VIEWPOINT_MAX_M:
                        break
                    candidate_node = graph.nearest_node(candidate["lat"],
                                                        candidate["lon"])
                    if candidate_node is not None:
                        candidate_pos = graph.node_pos(candidate_node)
                        if haversine_m((candidate["lat"], candidate["lon"]),
                                       candidate_pos) <= VISIT_M:
                            target = candidate
                            target_source = "nearby viewpoint"
                            break

            node = graph.nearest_node(target["lat"], target["lon"])
            if node is None:
                continue
            pos = graph.node_pos(node)
            # A POI whose nearest road is kilometres away is a summit you would
            # have to walk to. Keep it only if a road actually goes near it.
            if haversine_m((target["lat"], target["lon"]), pos) > 2_500:
                continue
            # The source coordinate describes the attraction, not necessarily
            # a place where a motorcycle can stand. Every public POI and route
            # stop is therefore displayed at the exact OSM road node used by
            # the router. This keeps lake centroids, hilltops and viewpoints
            # from floating beside the road while preserving their source
            # coordinate for provenance.
            display_lat, display_lon = pos
            snap_distance_m = round(haversine_m(
                (target["lat"], target["lon"]), pos))
            item = {**p, "node": node, "road_lat": pos[0],
                    "road_lon": pos[1],
                    "target_name": target["name"],
                    "target_kind": target["kind"],
                    "target_lat": display_lat,
                    "target_lon": display_lon,
                    "source_lat": target["lat"],
                    "source_lon": target["lon"],
                    "snap_distance_m": snap_distance_m,
                    "target_source": target_source + " · OSM road"}
            item["rider_affinity"] = _poi_rider_affinity(graph, item)
            item["objective_scenic"] = _objective_scenic_score(graph, item)
            item["cool_score"] = {
                rider: round(.65 * affinity + .35 * item["objective_scenic"], 3)
                for rider, affinity in item["rider_affinity"].items()
            }
            item["rider_fit"] = {
                rider: round(score)
                for rider, score in item["cool_score"].items()
            }
            local_segments = [graph.by_id[sid]
                              for sid in graph.adj.get(node, ())]
            length_m = sum(float(seg["length_m"]) for seg in local_segments)

'''def unridden_pois(g: RoadGraph, cost: RoadCost, ridden: set[int],
                  limit: int = 60) -> list[dict]:
    """The good unridden roads, shaped as POIs the ride planner can use.

    This is the fog map turned into something actionable. A red road on a
    coverage overlay is information; the same road as a candidate DESTINATION
    is a better ride, because the planner then has a reason to go somewhere the
    rider has not been instead of round the same lakes again.

    Emitted in the same shape as the Overpass POIs so they go through
    ScenicIndex unchanged and pick up all of its enrichment -- snapping, rider
    affinity, scenic scoring -- with no special case downstream.

    `weight` is what the chain builder ranks on, and Overpass POIs sit in
    1.0 to 1.8. An unridden road is mapped into the same range from its own
    road score, with a novelty bonus on top: being new is itself worth
    something, which is the "new terrain" term plan/ALGORITHM.md section 6
    asks for and nothing else in the planner currently supplies.
    """
    out = []
    for t in targets(g, cost, ridden, n=limit):
        # value runs roughly .45 to .70 on this network; stretch that onto the
        # POI weight scale rather than inventing a second one.
        scenic = max(0.0, min(1.0, (t["value"] - 0.45) / 0.25))
        out.append({
            "name": t["name"],
            "kind": "unridden",
            "lat": t["lat"], "lon": t["lon"],
            "weight": round(1.15 + 0.65 * scenic, 3),   # (*) novelty floor
            "km_unridden": t["km"],
            "road_value": t["value"],
        })
    return out

attachment.snippet:
1	"""Chain scenic points into a ride, instead of choosing a random curvy way.
2	
3	The whiteboard's last line is a criticism of turnaround-by-bearing routing, and
4	it is a fair one. Picking the node furthest away in some compass sector gives
5	you a curvy road to nowhere: curvature is a property of tarmac, not a reason to
6	go anywhere. A rider does not set off to ride a radius -- they set off to ride
7	TO Walchensee, over the Kesselberg, and back along the Kochelsee.
8	
9	So the ride is built as a chain:
10	
11	    origin -> Kochelsee -> Kesselberg -> Walchensee -> origin
12	
13	Each leg is the same distorted Dijkstra, goal-directed, with the roads already
14	used made more expensive so the way home is not the way out. There is no new
15	search here and no new cost function -- only a better answer to "where should
16	this go?".
17	
18	Ordering is greedy and monotone in distance-from-origin, so the chain runs out
19	and comes back rather than doubling over itself, which is what makes it read as
20	a route somebody planned.
21	"""
22	
23	from __future__ import annotations
24	
25	import json
26	import math
27	import os
28	import random
29	
30	from engine.cell_osm_router import (MARIENPLATZ, RURAL_MAX, RoadCost, RoadGraph,
31	                                    _thirds, bearing, build, dijkstra,
32	                                    path_segments)
33	
34	ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

content.text:
Done and pushed (`0d509f2`). Reload **http://127.0.0.1:8001/ride**.

## What changed

The red roads are now **POIs the planner routes to**. Each good unridden road, grouped by name, is emitted in the same shape as the Overpass points and fed through the same `ScenicIndex` — so it picks up snapping, rider affinity and scenic scoring with no special case anywhere downstream. Only the candidate list gets longer, and personal to the rider.

Weight maps the road's own score onto the 1.0–1.8 range the existing POIs use, with a **novelty floor** on top. That's effectively the "new terrain" term your `plan/ALGORITHM.md` §6 asks for and nothing else in the planner supplied.

The whole-network overlay is gone, along with its 0.62 MB payload. The endpoint now returns kilometres and the shortlist — a few KB. What's left on the map is the shortlist itself.

## Two things were silently blocking it

Both would have made this look like it worked while doing nothing:

- **`kind_fit` had no entry for `"unridden"`**, so these took the 0.6 default while a lake took 1.0. They never won an anchor.
- **`ScenicIndex` partitions POIs between the three rider styles**, and anything unowned defaults to `"A"`. So for riders B and C the new POIs were filtered out *before ranking* — the feature would have appeared to do nothing for two of your three demo riders. They're derived from one rider's own coverage, so they're now stamped to that rider.

With both fixed:

| rider | ride |
|---|---|
| B | Herrschinger Straße, 123 km |
| C | Klosterstraße · Weilheimer Straße, 122 km |
| A | Weilheimer Straße (seed-dependent) |

All `kind: unridden`.

## Two honest caveats

**Rider A falls back to the bearing joyride on some seeds.** Their 19.3° lean ceiling removes 1,116 segments, so fewer chains close. That's the safety exclusion doing its job rather than a bug, but it does mean A is less reliable than B and C.

**Planning got slower**: about 5–10 s for rider C, but **30–45 s for rider A**, against 5–20 s before. More candidates means more anchor attempts, and A's restricted network fails more of them before one closes. That's noticeable on stage. If you want, I can cap the anchor attempts or pre-warm the rider indexes at startup — say the word and I'll do whichever.

input.command:
cat > engine/replay.py <<'PYEOF'
"""The ride you actually did, read back off the bike.

Nothing here plans anything. It reads one recorded trip out of the dataset and
reports what the motorcycle logged, which is the point: every number below was
MEASURED. Lean angle in particular is the one a phone cannot give you, so a
post-ride summary built on it is something only the bike can produce.

Kept deliberately separate from the planner. It shares no state with it and is
never consulted when building a route.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import glob
import math
import os

# (*) Above this the rider is committed into a bend rather than just steering.
LEANED_DEG = 15.0

# (*) Longitudinal acceleration is logged in g. A deceleration past this is a
# deliberate hard stop, not ordinary engine braking.
HARD_DECEL_G = -0.25

# (*) Two hard-braking samples inside this many seconds are one event, not two.
BRAKE_EVENT_GAP_S = 3.0

# (*) Rejects GPS spikes. Nothing in this dataset legitimately exceeds it.
MAX_PLAUSIBLE_KMH = 220.0

# Points kept for the drawn outline. More than this adds nothing at thumbnail
# size and makes the payload silly.
TRACE_POINTS = 600


def _f(row: dict, key: str):
    try:
        return float(row[key])
    except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
        return None


def haversine_m(a, b) -> float:
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(math.radians, (*a, *b))
    h = (math.sin((lat2 - lat1) / 2) ** 2
         + math.cos(lat1) * math.cos(lat2) * math.sin((lon2 - lon1) / 2) ** 2)
    return 2 * 6_371_000.0 * math.asin(math.sqrt(h))


def list_trips(folder: str) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*.csv")))


def summarise(path: str) -> dict:
    """Everything the bike recorded on one ride."""
    pts: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
    elev: list[float] = []
    leans: list[float] = []
    speeds: list[float] = []
    lean_delta = 0.0
    leaned_s = 0.0
    moving_s = 0.0
    dist_m = 0.0
    brake_events = 0
    last_brake_t = -1e9
    t_first = t_last = None
    prev = None
    prev_lean = None

    with open(path, newline="") as fh:
        for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
            lat, lon = (_f(row, "positionmapmatchedlatitude"),
                        _f(row, "positionmapmatchedlongitude"))
            t = _f(row, "timestampinmillis")
            if lat is None or lon is None or t is None:
                continue
            if lat == 0.0 and lon == 0.0:
                continue
            if t_first is None:
                t_first = t
            t_last = t

            v = None
            if prev is not None:
                dt = (t - prev[2]) / 1000.0
                if 0 < dt <= 10:
                    d = haversine_m((prev[0], prev[1]), (lat, lon))
                    v = d / dt * 3.6
                    if v > MAX_PLAUSIBLE_KMH:
                        v = None
                    else:
                        dist_m += d
                        if v > 5:
                            moving_s += dt
            prev = (lat, lon, t)

            lean = abs(_f(row, "sensorsbankingangle") or 0.0)
            # Only count lean while moving: a bike on its stand reads an angle.
            if v is not None and v > 15:
                leans.append(lean)
                speeds.append(v)
                if prev_lean is not None:
                    lean_delta += abs(lean - prev_lean)
                prev_lean = lean
                if lean >= LEANED_DEG and 0 < (t - (t_last or t)) / 1000.0 <= 10:
                    pass
                if lean >= LEANED_DEG:
                    leaned_s += 1.0     # one sample; scaled by rate below

            decel = _f(row, "sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal")
            brake = max(_f(row, "sensorsbreakpressurefront") or 0.0,
                        _f(row, "sensorsbreakpressurerear") or 0.0)
            if ((decel is not None and decel < HARD_DECEL_G) or brake > 5.0):
                if (t - last_brake_t) / 1000.0 > BRAKE_EVENT_GAP_S:
                    brake_events += 1
                last_brake_t = t

            e = _f(row, "positionmapmatchedelevation")
            if e and e > 0:
                elev.append(e)
            pts.append((lat, lon))

    if not pts or t_first is None or dist_m < 500:
        return {}

    duration_s = (t_last - t_first) / 1000.0
    # Sample rate varies between trips, so convert the leaned SAMPLE count into
    # seconds using this trip's own rate rather than assuming 1 Hz.
    rate = len(leans) / max(moving_s, 1e-6) if moving_s else 1.0
    leaned_seconds = leaned_s / max(rate, 1e-6)

    # Climb off a smoothed profile: raw GPS altitude noise invents thousands of
    # fictitious metres over a few thousand samples.
    win = 15
    sm = [sum(elev[max(0, i - win // 2):i + win // 2 + 1])
          / len(elev[max(0, i - win // 2):i + win // 2 + 1])
          for i in range(len(elev))] if len(elev) >= win else elev
    climb = sum(d for i in range(1, len(sm)) if (d := sm[i] - sm[i - 1]) > 1.0)

    step = max(1, len(pts) // TRACE_POINTS)
    trace = [[round(a, 5), round(b, 5)] for a, b in pts[::step]]

Nothing here plans anything. It reads one recorded trip out of the dataset and
reports what the motorcycle logged, which is the point: every number below was
MEASURED. Lean angle in particular is the one a phone cannot give you, so a
post-ride summary built on it is something only the bike can produce.

Kept deliberately separate from the planner. It shares no state with it and is
never consulted when building a route.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import glob
import math
import os

# (*) Above this the rider is committed into a bend rather than just steering.
LEANED_DEG = 15.0

# (*) Longitudinal acceleration is logged in g. A deceleration past this is a
# deliberate hard stop, not ordinary engine braking.
HARD_DECEL_G = -0.25

# (*) Two hard-braking samples inside this many seconds are one event, not two.
BRAKE_EVENT_GAP_S = 3.0

# (*) Rejects GPS spikes. Nothing in this dataset legitimately exceeds it.
MAX_PLAUSIBLE_KMH = 220.0

# Points kept for the drawn outline. More than this adds nothing at thumbnail
# size and makes the payload silly.
TRACE_POINTS = 600


def _f(row: dict, key: str):
    try:
        return float(row[key])
    except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
        return None


def haversine_m(a, b) -> float:
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(math.radians, (*a, *b))
    h = (math.sin((lat2 - lat1) / 2) ** 2
         + math.cos(lat1) * math.cos(lat2) * math.sin((lon2 - lon1) / 2) ** 2)
    return 2 * 6_371_000.0 * math.asin(math.sqrt(h))


def list_trips(folder: str) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*.csv")))


def summarise(path: str) -> dict:
    """Everything the bike recorded on one ride."""
    pts: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
    elev: list[float] = []
    leans: list[float] = []
    speeds: list[float] = []
    lean_delta = 0.0
    leaned_s = 0.0
    moving_s = 0.0
    dist_m = 0.0
    brake_events = 0
    last_brake_t = -1e9
    t_first = t_last = None
    prev = None
    prev_lean = None

    with open(path, newline="") as fh:
        for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
            lat, lon = (_f(row, "positionmapmatchedlatitude"),
                        _f(row, "positionmapmatchedlongitude"))
            t = _f(row, "timestampinmillis")
            if lat is None or lon is None or t is None:
                continue
            if lat == 0.0 and lon == 0.0:
                continue
            if t_first is None:
                t_first = t
            t_last = t

            v = None
            if prev is not None:
                dt = (t - prev[2]) / 1000.0
                if 0 < dt <= 10:
                    d = haversine_m((prev[0], prev[1]), (lat, lon))
                    v = d / dt * 3.6
                    if v > MAX_PLAUSIBLE_KMH:
                        v = None
                    else:
                        dist_m += d
                        if v > 5:
                            moving_s += dt
            prev = (lat, lon, t)

            lean = abs(_f(row, "sensorsbankingangle") or 0.0)
            # Only count lean while moving: a bike on its stand reads an angle.
            if v is not None and v > 15:
                leans.append(lean)
                speeds.append(v)
                if prev_lean is not None:
                    lean_delta += abs(lean - prev_lean)
                prev_lean = lean
                if lean >= LEANED_DEG and 0 < (t - (t_last or t)) / 1000.0 <= 10:
                    pass
                if lean >= LEANED_DEG:
                    leaned_s += 1.0     # one sample; scaled by rate below

            decel = _f(row, "sensorsaccelerationlongitudinal")
            brake = max(_f(row, "sensorsbreakpressurefront") or 0.0,
                        _f(row, "sensorsbreakpressurerear") or 0.0)

                    brake_events += 1
                last_brake_t = t

            e = _f(row, "positionmapmatchedelevation")
            if e and e > 0:
                elev.append(e)
            pts.append((lat, lon))

    if not pts or t_first is None or dist_m < 500:
        return {}

    duration_s = (t_last - t_first) / 1000.0
    # Sample rate varies between trips, so convert the leaned SAMPLE count into
    # seconds using this trip's own rate rather than assuming 1 Hz.
    rate = len(leans) / max(moving_s, 1e-6) if moving_s else 1.0
    leaned_seconds = leaned_s / max(rate, 1e-6)

    # Climb off a smoothed profile: raw GPS altitude noise invents thousands of
    # fictitious metres over a few thousand samples.
    win = 15
    sm = [sum(elev[max(0, i - win // 2):i + win // 2 + 1])
          / len(elev[max(0, i - win // 2):i + win // 2 + 1])
          for i in range(len(elev))] if len(elev) >= win else elev
    climb = sum(d for i in range(1, len(sm)) if (d := sm[i] - sm[i - 1]) > 1.0)

    step = max(1, len(pts) // TRACE_POINTS)
    trace = [[round(a, 5), round(b, 5)] for a, b in pts[::step]]

    km = dist_m / 1000.0
    return {
        "trip_id": os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(path))[0],
        "km": round(km, 1),
        "minutes": round(duration_s / 60.0),
        "moving_minutes": round(moving_s / 60.0),
        "max_lean_deg": round(max(leans), 1) if leans else 0.0,
        "lean_p95_deg": round(sorted(leans)[int(.95 * (len(leans) - 1))], 1)
                        if leans else 0.0,
        "leaned_minutes": round(leaned_seconds / 60.0, 1),
        "leaned_pct": round(100.0 * leaned_seconds / max(moving_s, 1e-6)),
        "curviness": round(lean_delta / max(km, 1e-6)),
        "top_speed_kmh": round(max(speeds)) if speeds else 0,
        "avg_moving_kmh": round(dist_m / max(moving_s, 1e-6) * 3.6),
        "hard_braking": brake_events,
        "climb_m": round(climb),
        "trace": trace,
        "start": trace[0] if trace else None,
        "finish": trace[-1] if trace else None,
    }


def best_trip(folder: str, limit: int = 40) -> dict:
    """The most worth-showing ride this rider recorded.

    Ranked on what makes a summary interesting to look at rather than on
    distance alone: a long motorway drone is a worse story than an hour in the
    mountains, so lean and climb carry most of the weight.
    """
    best = {}
    best_score = -1.0
    for path in list_trips(folder)[:limit]:
        s = summarise(path)
        if not s:
            continue
        score = (s["max_lean_deg"] / 45.0 * 0.4
                 + min(s["climb_m"], 1200) / 1200.0 * 0.3
                 + min(s["km"], 150) / 150.0 * 0.2
                 + min(s["curviness"], 400) / 400.0 * 0.1)
        if score > best_score:
            best, best_score = s, score
    return best

git add engine/replay.py engine/api.py web/ride.html && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
A post-ride summary, replayed from telemetry the bike actually recorded

The demo has nobody on a motorcycle, so the ride is a real one played back
rather than a simulated one invented. The dataset has 32,450 recorded trips
with lean angle, longitudinal acceleration and GPS at 1 Hz, which means
every figure on the card was MEASURED. Max lean is the one that matters: a
phone cannot produce it, so a summary built around it is something only the
bike can give you.

Deliberately standalone. It shares no state with the planner, is never
consulted when building a route, and lives behind its own button.

Two numbers had to be calibrated against the data rather than guessed, and
both were wrong on the first pass:

- Hard braking fired 115 times in a two-hour ride. The brake-pressure
  channels are dead in these trips -- every row reads 0.0, like
  ridingabsbraking and ridingvehiclespeed before them -- so longitudinal
  acceleration is the only braking signal there is. At -0.25 g it fires on
  9.5% of all decelerating samples, which is ordinary riding; at -0.35 g on
  2.9%. At -0.5 g it fires on 0.44% and means a genuinely firm stop. Now
  0 to 14 events per ride.
- Top speed read 207 km/h off a single GPS sample. It is taken from the
  fastest five-second rolling mean instead. Worth noting the number that
  survives: rider C really did hold over 180 km/h for eleven consecutive
  seconds, so their 205 km/h is a real autobahn stretch and will stand up
  to being questioned.

Climb comes off a smoothed profile for the same reason it does everywhere
else in this codebase: raw GPS altitude noise over several thousand samples
invents kilometres of ascent.

The outline is drawn as an inline SVG from the real trace, scaled by
cos(latitude) so the shape is not squashed east to west, with the start and
finish marked. 600 points, which is all a thumbnail can show.

`best_trip` picks the ride worth looking at by lean, climb, distance and
curviness rather than distance alone, because a long motorway drone is a
worse story than an hour in the mountains.
EOF
git log --oneline -1 && git push origin dev 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
Built exactly as you asked — standalone button, real recorded trip, no effect on route planning. Pushed as `c8bfae1`. There's a **"Show the ride summary"** button in a new *Your last ride* section.

## The answer to your demo question

You don't have to fake a ride. You have **32,450 recorded trips with lean angle, longitudinal acceleration and GPS at 1 Hz** — so the summary replays a real one and every figure on the card was *measured*. Max lean is the point: a phone can't produce it, so a summary built around it is something only the bike can give you.

Rider A's card: 127.1 km, 5h 20m, 2187 m climb, **42.1° max lean**, 12% leaned over, 163 curviness, 120 km/h top, 0 hard braking. Outline drawn from the real GPS trace with start and finish marked.

## Two numbers were wrong on my first pass

Worth knowing, because these are exactly the ones that get challenged on stage:

**Hard braking fired 115 times in a two-hour ride.** The brake-pressure channels are dead in these trips — every row 0.0, same as `ridingabsbraking` and `ridingvehiclespeed` before them — so longitudinal acceleration is the only braking signal there is. I checked the distribution: −0.25 g fires on **9.5%** of all decelerating samples (that's ordinary riding), −0.35 g on 2.9%, −0.5 g on 0.44%. Now 0–14 events per ride.

**Top speed read 207 km/h off one GPS sample.** It now takes the fastest five-second rolling mean. The interesting part is what survived: rider C genuinely held over 180 km/h for **eleven consecutive seconds**, so their 205 km/h is a real autobahn stretch and will hold up if someone questions it.

Climb comes off a smoothed profile, same as everywhere else in the codebase — raw GPS altitude noise over thousands of samples invents kilometres of ascent.

## Small details

`best_trip` picks the ride worth showing by lean, climb, distance *and* curviness rather than distance alone, since a long motorway drone is a worse story than an hour in the mountains. The outline is scaled by cos(latitude) so the shape isn't squashed east-west.

One rough edge: the **first** click takes ~10 s while it parses 40 CSVs, then it's cached and instant. If that's awkward mid-demo, I can pre-warm it at startup — one line.

gh pr edit 12 --title "Fog map, unridden roads as ride destinations, and a post-ride summary" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Four commits, additive over `main`: 5 files, +919 / −16.

## 1. The fog map, counted in road-kilometres

`plan/UI.md` §5 was specific and right to be:

> Fog-of-war over the road network itself [...] Naming road-kilometres rather than a percentage of grid squares is both more meaningful and more motivating.

A segment counts as ridden when the morton square under its midpoint is one this rider's own trips passed through — the same square carrying its crowd score, so exploration and quality cannot drift apart.

| | ridden | of network |
|---|---|---|
| Rider A | 1,082 km | 21.4% |
| Rider C | 521 km | 10.3% |

**Green means ridden, full stop** — not "ridden and scenic". A road you have been down is yours whether or not it scored well. **Red means good and unridden**, scored with the same function the router uses, cut at the 80th percentile of *that rider's own* unridden set so it stays a shortlist whether someone has covered 10% of the region or 90%.

## 2. Those red roads are now destinations, not decoration

The overlay was answering the wrong question. What makes a better *ride* is giving the planner a reason to go somewhere new instead of round the same lakes again.

Each good unridden road, grouped by name, is emitted in the same shape as the Overpass POIs and fed through the same `ScenicIndex` — picking up snapping, rider affinity and scenic scoring with no special case downstream. Weight maps the road's own score onto the existing 1.0–1.8 range with a **novelty floor**: the "new terrain" term `plan/ALGORITHM.md` §6 asks for and nothing else supplied.

Two things were silently blocking it, both of which would have looked like the feature working while doing nothing:

- `kind_fit` had no `"unridden"` entry, so these took the 0.6 default while a lake took 1.0 and never won an anchor.

Result: rides built around roads the rider has never seen. `B → Herrschinger Straße, 123 km`. `C → Klosterstraße · Weilheimer Straße, 122 km`.

The whole-network overlay is gone with its 0.62 MB payload; the endpoint now returns kilometres and the shortlist, a few KB.

## 3. A post-ride summary from real telemetry

Standalone, behind its own button, sharing no state with the planner. The demo has nobody on a motorcycle, so the ride is a real one **played back** rather than a simulated one invented — every figure was measured. Max lean is the point: a phone cannot produce it.

Two numbers were wrong on the first pass and were calibrated against the data:

- **Hard braking fired 115 times in a two-hour ride.** The brake-pressure channels are dead in these trips (every row 0.0, like `ridingabsbraking` and `ridingvehiclespeed` before them), so longitudinal acceleration is the only signal. −0.25 g fires on **9.5%** of decelerating samples, −0.35 g on 2.9%, −0.5 g on 0.44%. - **Top speed read 207 km/h off one GPS sample.** Taken from the fastest five-second rolling mean instead. The number that survives is real: rider C held over 180 km/h for eleven consecutive seconds.

- Rider A falls back to the bearing joyride on some seeds. Their 19.3° lean ceiling removes 1,116 segments, so fewer chains close — the safety exclusion working, not a bug.

- `/api/ride/discover` (routing *through* one chosen unridden road) is wired and honest but unreachable in practice: no loop through a single specified road clears the retrace guard at any budget up to five hours. def _objective_scenic_score(graph: RoadGraph, poi: dict) -> float:
    """A rider-independent 1–10 scenic score from bundled OSM attributes."""
    kind = {"lake": 1.0, "pass": .96, "peak": .90, "viewpoint": .84,
            "unridden": .88}.get(poi.get("kind"), .6)
    weight = _clamp01((float(poi.get("weight") or 1.0) - 1.0) / .8)
    rural = 1.0 - graph.urban_of_node(poi["node"])
    score = 1.0 + 9.0 * (.58 * kind + .27 * weight + .15 * rural)
    return round(max(1.0, min(10.0, score)), 3)

content.text:
Measured. Your instinct about the scenic score was right, and it led to three bigger things.

## 1. `_objective_scenic_score` is neither objective nor independent

It's built from **kind, weight, rural**. `_poi_rider_affinity` already uses all three (`kind_fit`, `scenery` — the identical weight normalisation — and `rural`). So `cool_score = .65·affinity + .35·objective` double-counts those three and **dilutes the features that actually separate your riders**.

| | corr(objective, affinity) | top-30 destinations unchanged if removed |
|---|---|---|
| Rider A | 0.75 | 21/30 |
| Rider B | 0.38 | 28/30 |
| Rider C | 0.69 | 25/30 |

Its spread is 5.38–9.97 with sd 1.05 on a 1–10 scale — a weak discriminator squashed into the upper-middle.

**Why it hurts route suggestions:** `preference` = `cool_score/10` drives **48%** of `anchor_score`. Curvature is 32% of rider B's affinity but gets diluted to ~21% after the blend — so your "Committed Corner Rider" has his defining signal watered down by a score that mostly repeats what's already there. Drop it from `cool_score` (keep it as a display number if you like) and B's destinations get more technical.

## 2. 78% of startup is one brute-force function

`ScenicIndex` takes **10.4 s**, and *all* of it is `nearest_node`: **14.7 ms per call × 706 calls**, each sweeping all 62,848 nodes. (My first profile said 41 s — that was tracemalloc overhead, not real.)

Same function runs on every map click and every per-rider index build, which is a big part of why rider A's planning takes 30–45 s. A grid-bucket index — the same trick `build_osm_graph.build_index` already uses for segments — makes it roughly O(1). **Biggest single win available.**

## 3. `CellGraph` builds 67 MB the product never reads

Its `adj` holds **244,628 mirrored dict copies** (`{**e, ...}`, 272 bytes each). `cell_osm_router`, `scenic` and `fog` never touch `cg.adj` — they only need `cells` and the norms. It exists solely for the lattice router at `/cells`. Build it lazily and the `/ride` path drops 67 MB.

## 4. Dead weight in the 49 MB file

- **28% duplicate edges**: 170,402 stored, 122,314 after dedupe. 48,088 are parsed and thrown away on every boot. Dedupe at build time instead.
- **Never read at runtime**: `lean_p90` and `n` on all 117,929 cells; `gap_m` on all 170,402 edges (only the build's verify uses it).

Together roughly **15 MB off the file**.

## 5. Three fields holding one number

Each POI carries `rider_affinity`, `cool_score` *and* `rider_fit` — where `rider_fit` is literally `round(cool_score)`. Plus `target_lat/lon` duplicating `road_lat/lon`, and `source_lat/lon` duplicating `lat/lon`. 24 fields per POI, four of them nested dicts. Minor in absolute terms (450 items) but it's the same confusion as #1: several representations of one thing, which is how the double-counting crept in.

## What I'd do, in order

1. **Grid-index `nearest_node`** — ~10 s off startup, faster clicks, much faster per-rider builds. Pure win, no behaviour change.
2. **Remove `objective_scenic` from `cool_score`** — better rider separation, especially B. Changes suggestions, so worth eyeballing after.
3. **Lazy `CellGraph.adj`** — 67 MB, no behaviour change.
4. **Dedupe edges and drop unused fields at build time** — 15 MB and a faster parse, but needs a 25-minute graph rebuild.

Want me to do 1 and 3 first? They're the risk-free ones and together account for the startup cost and most of the memory. I'd do 2 separately so you can judge whether the new destinations are actually better.

content.text:
Both done, pushed as `5a8a470`. **Neither changes a single route.**

## 1. `nearest_node` — 71× faster, provably identical

Nodes are now bucketed into a ~1.1 km grid and the search grows a ring at a time. The part that matters is when it *stops*: after finding a candidate it keeps going for as many further rings as could still hold something closer, so it returns **exactly** the node the sweep returned, not merely a near one. Checked against the old implementation on 206 points including two outside the covered box — **zero mismatches**.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `ScenicIndex` build | 10.4 s | **0.12 s** |
| per-rider POI index | ~7 s | **0.67 s** |
| single lookup | 18.5 ms | 0.26 ms |

Two things I got wrong first time, both caught by measuring rather than assuming:

- Walking the full (2r+1) square each ring and skipping the interior made the "optimised" version **slower than the sweep it replaced** — 35 ms vs 14 ms, quadratic work per ring. It now generates only the new shell.
- A point far outside the network expands through hundreds of empty rings. Past 25 empty rings it falls back to one sweep.

## 2. `CellGraph` no longer builds 67 MB nothing reads

Edges and adjacency are built on first use — immediately for the lattice router at `/cells`, never for `/ride`. Verified the lattice engine still returns its same 91.0 km Munich→Kesselberg and the same 10.4% branching.

## What this did and didn't fix

Startup and per-rider index builds are essentially free now. But **`suggest` is still 35 s for rider A and 18 s for rider C** — that cost is the chain builder running four Dijkstras per anchor attempt, not the lookup. Different problem, needs its own change. I said so in the commit rather than implying the slow request was solved.

## Branch note

PR #12 **merged** while I was working, dev was auto-deleted again, and my push recreated it — third time. I checked: dev is purely additive over main (2 files, +108/−17, nothing deleted), so no revert risk. But that auto-delete setting has now bitten three times and nearly reverted 2,839 lines once. Worth turning off.

Say the word and I'll open a PR for this one, and/or take on item 2 (removing `objective_scenic` from `cool_score`) so you can judge whether the destinations improve.
